sections.title: Reading Comprehension · Passage B
sections.intro: This poem was written by a revered 8th-century Chinese poet. Read “A Dream of Mountaineering” and answer questions 11–14. Vocabulary notes follow the poem.

passage.title: A Dream of Mountaineering
passage.credit: —Po Chü–I · “A Dream of Mountaineering” · from A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), translated by Arthur Waley, Constable and Company Ltd.

lines.text: At night, in my dream, I stoutly climbed a mountain,
Going out alone with my staff of holly-wood.¹
A thousand crags, a hundred hundred valleys—
In my dream-journey none were unexplored
And all the while my feet never grew tired
And my step was as strong as in my young days.
Can it be that when the mind travels backward
The body also returns to its old state?
And can it be, as between body and soul,
That the body may languish, while the soul is still strong?
In the day my feet are palsied³ and tottering;
In the night my steps go striding over the hills.
As day and night are divided in equal parts—
Between the two, I *get* as much as I *lose*.
¹ staff of holly-wood — a walking stick

questions.prompt: Lines 5 and 13 serve to emphasize a contrast between
questions.explanation: In the dream, the speaker’s feet never tire; by day, they shake and stagger. The contrast separates the dream’s illusion of youthful strength from waking reality.

questions.prompt: As used in line 10, “languish” most nearly means
questions.explanation: The speaker contrasts a body weakened by age with a soul that still feels strong. “Languish” means the body deteriorates or loses vigor.

questions.prompt: Lines 15 and 16 suggest that “day and night”
questions.explanation: The speaker loses physical strength during waking daylight but regains freedom of movement in dreams. Dividing life between day and night lets him gain as much as he loses.

questions.prompt: The tone of the poem can best be described as
questions.explanation: The speaker thoughtfully compares his dream journeys with his daytime limitations and asks what they mean for body and soul. That questioning creates a reflective tone.
